To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the extinction of Cretaceous marine planktonic foramifers at the KTB is a sudden event that occurred within a few hundred years, and that the proportion of survivors is 22% (or 11% if only P1a is considered).
the KTB at the El Kef section was a sudden biotic turnover, and that the diversity of plankton foraminifers declined by 50% across the boundary, and by 90% into zone P1b.

the diversity decline of planktonic Foraminifers across the KT boundary is more gradual than previously thought, but still more sudden than the background rate of diversity decline, and that the proportion of survivors is lower than previously thought, although still higher than in many previous studies.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the fossil record is not as reliable as we would wish, but that the KTB is a good place to study biotic turnover because the boundary is well dated and the boundary clay is a global time plane.

the fossil record of biotic turnover is distorted by the Signor-Lipps and Jaanusssohn effects, and that the record of the planktonic foramins across the KTB shows a sudden and severe decline in diversity.
we should not overinterpret patterns of biotic change, but rather focus on the timing and severity of the biotic turnover, and not be too quick to invoke environmental change to explain it.
